title: Why a tiny C project still needs a header file
description:
This C contact book is split across three files, and the header is the part beginners find confusing. contacts.h holds only the Contact struct and the function prototypes -- no logic. contacts.c holds the bodies. That's the interface/implementation split that every large C codebase is built on.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/10-project-contact-book/

#Shorts

beats.narration: One contact book, three files. Feels like overkill, until you see what each file is actually for. The header is the part that trips people up.
contacts dot h holds zero logic. Just the Contact struct and five function prototypes. It's a promise: here's what exists and how to call it.
contacts dot c is where the bodies live. Same signature as the header, now with the real loop doing the work. Rewrite this and nothing else has to change.
You hand both C files to gcc. main dot c only ever included the header, so it built against the promise, not the details.
That's the interface and implementation split. The header is the contract, the C file is how it's kept. Big C codebases are just this, repeated.
